questions.prompt: For a gradient step of length \(t\) and a gradient Lipschitz constant \(L\), the sufficient-decrease lemma gives
options: an increase of size \(t \lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\) for every \(t > 0\)
\(f(x) - f(x - t \nabla f(x)) \ge t(1 - L t/2)\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\) when \(0 < t < 2/L\)
questions.explanation:
Insert \(y = x - t 
abla f\) into the descent lemma. The linear term contributes \(-t \lVert
abla fVert^2\) and the quadratic term contributes \((L/2) t^2 \lVert
abla fVert^2\). The difference is \(t(1 - L t/2)\lVert
abla fVert^2\), which is positive for \(t \in (0, 2/L)\). A longer step can make the coefficient negative. The function value is not frozen.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Let \(L = 4\), \(t = 1/4\), and \(\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2 = 16\). What decrease does the lemma guarantee?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is \(t(1 - L t/2) = (1/4)(1 - 4 \cdot (1/4) / 2) = (1/4)(1 - 1/2) = 1/8\). Then \((1/8) \cdot 16 = 2\). Reporting \(16\) is the squared gradient norm. Reporting \(4\) is \(L\). Reporting \(1/8\) is the coefficient before it multiplies the squared norm.

questions.prompt: Among constant steps, the coefficient \(t(1 - L t/2)\) is largest at
questions.explanation: The map \(t \mapsto t - (L/2) t^2\) is a downward parabola. Its vertex is at \(t = 1/L\), and the value there is \(1/(2L)\). At \(t = 2/L\) the coefficient is zero, so the lemma guarantees nothing. The step \(t = L\) is far past \(2/L\) whenever \(L > \sqrt{2}\), and it is not the vertex in any case. At \(t = 0\) the coefficient is zero.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that derives the sufficient decrease of a gradient step. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The descent lemma is the inequality being specialized, so the gradient step has to be substituted first. The linear term and then the quadratic term are what that substitution produces. Factoring collects them, and the sign of the collected coefficient is the last reading. Declaring a range for \(t\) before the coefficient exists has nothing to sign.

steps: Insert \(y = x - t \nabla f(x)\) into the descent lemma.
Simplify the linear term to \(-t \lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\).
Simplify the quadratic term to \((L/2) t^2 \lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\).
Factor the decrease as \(t(1 - L t/2)\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\).
Conclude that the decrease is positive when \(0 < t < 2/L\).

questions.prompt: Let \(L = 4\). Which step lengths make the lemma guarantee a strict decrease of a gradient step with nonzero gradient?
questions.explanation:
The coefficient \(t(1 - 4 t/2) = t(1 - 2t)\) is positive for \(0 < t < 1/2\).
• The steps \(1/4\), \(1/10\), and \(2/5\) lie in that open interval.
• The step \(1/2\) equals \(2/L\), so the guaranteed decrease is zero.
• The step \(1\) is larger than \(1/2\), so the coefficient is negative and the lemma gives no decrease.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The step length is \(t\), the Lipschitz constant is \(\mathrm{ell}\), and the squared gradient norm is \(s\). The decrease guaranteed by the lemma equals
questions.explanation: The factored decrease is \(t(1 - \mathrm{ell}\, t/2)\) times the squared gradient norm. All three names appear. Dropping the term \(\mathrm{ell}\, t/2\) leaves the pure linear prediction \(t s\), which the quadratic remainder can spoil. Using \(t(1 + \mathrm{ell}\, t/2) s\) adds the remainder instead of subtracting it. Dividing by \(s\) reports a coefficient rather than a decrease.

questions.prompt: A note derives the decrease of a gradient step from the descent lemma. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation:
The substitution into an upper bound is the right starting point, the linear contribution is \(-t \lVert
abla fVert^2\), and the quadratic contribution is \((L/2) t^2 \lVert
abla fVert^2\). Subtracting the new upper bound from \(f(x)\) produces \(t \lVert
abla fVert^2 - (L/2) t^2 \lVert
abla fVert^2\), which factors as \(t(1 - L t/2)\lVert
abla fVert^2\). The false step adds the quadratic term instead of subtracting it.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: The descent lemma supplies an upper bound on \(f(x - t \nabla f)\).
The quadratic term contributes \((L/2) t^2 \lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\).
The guaranteed decrease is therefore \(t(1 + L t/2)\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\).
reasons: The quadratic term is subtracted. The factor is \(1 - L t/2\), not \(1 + L t/2\).
The descent lemma is a lower bound on the new value.

questions.prompt: Let \(L = 5\), \(t = 1/5\), and \(\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2 = 10\). What decrease does the lemma guarantee?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is \((1/5)(1 - 5 \cdot (1/5) / 2) = (1/5)(1/2) = 1/10\). Then \((1/10) \cdot 10 = 1\). This is the step \(t = 1/L\), whose coefficient is \(1/(2L) = 1/10\). Reporting \(10\) is the squared norm. Reporting \(5\) is \(L\). Reporting \(1/10\) is the coefficient alone.

questions.prompt: For the direction \(d = -\nabla f\), the descent-lemma decrease implies the Armijo test with parameter \(c \in (0, 1)\) whenever
questions.explanation:
Armijo along \(d = -
abla f\) asks for a decrease of at least \(c t \lVert
abla fVert^2\). The lemma supplies \(t(1 - L t/2)\lVert
abla fVert^2\). The lemma's coefficient is at least \(c t\) when \(1 - L t/2 \ge c\), which rearranges to \(t \le 2(1 - c)/L\). A step past \(2/L\) is outside the lemma's decrease regime. The parameter \(c\) stays below 1. The gradient norm is not \(c\).

questions.prompt: Summing this decrease along a sequence of gradient steps is the start of
options: a convergence argument: the sum of the squared gradient norms stays bounded
a proof that the step length must grow
a proof that the Hessian is indefinite
questions.explanation: Each step removes at least a fixed multiple of \(\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\) from the function value. If \(f\) is bounded below, the sum of those decreases is finite, so the sum of the squared gradient norms is finite. That is the opening of the convergence argument. It does not force the step length to grow. The ratio test and an indefinite Hessian are different subjects.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: Let \(L = 5\). What is \(2/L\), the step length at which the lemma's guaranteed decrease drops to zero?
questions.explanation: Divide \(2\) by \(5\). The threshold is \(0.4\). For every \(t \in (0, 0.4)\) the coefficient \(t(1 - L t/2)\) is positive, and at \(t = 0.4\) it is zero. Reporting \(5\) is \(L\). Reporting \(0.2\) is \(1/L\), the step that maximizes the coefficient rather than the step that kills it. Reporting \(2.5\) is \(L/2\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A projected gradient step keeps this decrease when the projection is
options: allowed to increase distances without any change to the proof
replaced by an unconstrained Newton step
computed from a simplex basis of a linear program
nonexpansive, so the same Lipschitz argument still controls the accepted step
questions.explanation: The sufficient-decrease algebra uses the length of the step that was actually taken. A Euclidean projection does not increase distances, so a projected step is no longer than the unprojected gradient step it came from, and the same \(L\) still closes the estimate. A map that stretches distances would need a new argument. Newton and the simplex method are different iterations.
